from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Prerequisite: The Concept of Distributions", [
            "Data shapes aren't always bell-shaped.",
            "Some distributions are uniform or skewed.",
            "Most real-world data is messy."
        ])
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Data shapes aren't always bell-shaped.
        uniform_box = Rectangle(width=2, height=1, color="#FF5733")
        normal_curve = FunctionGraph(lambda x: np.exp(-x**2), x_range=[-2, 2], color="#33FF57")
        
        self.place_at_grid(uniform_box, 'B2', scale_factor=0.5)
        self.place_at_grid(normal_curve, 'B5', scale_factor=0.5)
        
        label_u = Text("Uniform", color="#FF5733", font_size=20).next_to(uniform_box, UP)
        label_n = Text("Normal", color="#33FF57", font_size=20).next_to(normal_curve, UP)
        
        self.play(Create(uniform_box), Create(normal_curve), Write(label_u), Write(label_n))
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FFD700")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Some distributions are uniform or skewed.
        skewed_curve = FunctionGraph(lambda x: (x+2)**2 * np.exp(-x-2), x_range=[-2, 3], color="#FF33FF")
        self.place_at_grid(skewed_curve, 'E3', scale_factor=0.4)
        label_s = Text("Skewed", color="#FF33FF", font_size=20).next_to(skewed_curve, UP)
        
        self.play(Create(skewed_curve), Write(label_s))
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FFD700")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Most real-world data is messy.
        dots = VGroup(*[Dot(color=WHITE, radius=0.03) for _ in range(50)])
        for dot in dots:
            dot.move_to(self.grid['E5'] + np.random.uniform(-0.5, 0.5, 3))
        
        real_world_text = Text("Real-world data", color=WHITE, font_size=24)
        self.place_at_grid(real_world_text, 'D5', scale_factor=0.8)
        
        self.play(FadeIn(dots), Write(real_world_text))
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#FFD700")
        self.wait(2)

class Section2Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = ["We often need population parameters.", "Surveying everyone is impossible.", "Sample means reveal order in chaos."]
        self.setup_layout("The Core Problem: Why Sample Means?", lecture_lines)

        YELLOW = "#FFFF33"

        sample_box = Square(color=WHITE, side_length=2.0)
        self.place_in_area(sample_box, "A4", "C6")
        label = Text("Sample", font_size=16).next_to(sample_box, UP)
        self.play(FadeIn(acorn), Create(circle), Create(sample_box), Write(label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color(YELLOW)
        pop_box = Rectangle(color=WHITE, width=4, height=3)
        self.place_in_area(pop_box, "D1", "F6")
        pop_label = Text("Population", font_size=18).next_to(pop_box, UP)
        self.play(FadeIn(pop_box), Write(pop_label))
        
        # Highlight selection
        selections = VGroup(*[Dot(color=YELLOW) for _ in range(5)])

        self.play(FadeIn(selections))

class Section5Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Real-World Application & Summary", [
            "CLT bridges probability and statistics.", 
            "We infer populations from small samples.", 
            "It is the backbone of inference."
        ])
        
        # --- Assets ---
        # 1. Conveyor / Robot / Bulbs
        conveyor = Line(start=self.grid["F2"], end=self.grid["F6"], color=GRAY)
        bulb = Circle(radius=0.2, color=YELLOW, fill_opacity=0.8)
        
        # 2. Bridge / Confidence Interval
        bridge = VGroup(
            Line(self.grid["D2"], self.grid["D6"], color=WHITE),
            Text("Population", font_size=18).move_to(self.grid["E4"]),
            Text("Sample", font_size=18).move_to(self.grid["C4"])
        )
        ci_bracket = Brace(Line(self.grid["C2"], self.grid["C6"]), color="#33FFFF")
        ci_text = ci_bracket.get_text("Confidence Interval").scale(0.8).set_color("#33FFFF")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(BLUE)
        self.add(conveyor)
        self.play(FadeIn(bulb), run_time=1)
        self.play(Create(bridge), FadeIn(ci_bracket), FadeIn(ci_text), run_time=2)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color(BLUE)
        formula = MathTex(r"\bar{x} \pm z \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}", font_size=32)
        self.place_at_grid(formula, "B3")
        self.play(Write(formula), run_time=2)
        self.play(Indicate(ci_bracket), run_time=1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color(BLUE)
        final_label = Text("CLT: The Bridge", font_size=36, color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(final_label, "A3")
        self.play(FadeIn(final_label), run_time=1)
        self.play(final_label.animate.set_color("#FFFFFF").scale(1.2), run_time=1)
        self.wait(2)

outline.topic: The Central Limit Theorem (CLT): From Chaos to Order

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Concept of Distributions
sections.content: Briefly define what a probability distribution is. Contrast a 'Normal Distribution' (Bell Curve) with 'Non-Normal Distributions' (Uniform or Skewed) using visual icons. Establish that real-world data is often messy and non-normal.
sections.example: Visualizing a die roll (Uniform distribution) vs. human height (Normal distribution).

sections.title: The Core Problem: Why Sample Means?
sections.content: Introduce the motivation: We want to estimate population parameters. Explain that while individual data points are erratic, the 'average' of samples behaves differently. Set the stage for the CLT transition.
sections.example: An anthropomorphic 'Survey Squirrel' trying to estimate the average weight of acorns in a forest without weighing every single one.

sections.title: The CLT Mechanism (Visual Experiment)
sections.content: Explain the step-by-step process: 1. Take a large number of random samples from any population. 2. Calculate the mean of each sample. 3. Plot these means. Use an animation showing a jagged, non-normal distribution collapsing into a smooth Bell Curve as sample size (n) increases.
sections.example: Animation: 1000 trials of a 'Survey Squirrel' picking 30 acorns, recording the average weight, and repeating, resulting in a perfect Bell Curve.

sections.title: Critical Knowledge Points
sections.content: Define the two pillars: 1. Shape: The distribution of sample means approaches Normal regardless of the original distribution. 2. Sample Size: The magic number (usually n ≥ 30) where the effect becomes statistically significant.
sections.example: A graphic 'Scale of Stability' showing the curve sharpening from 'Unreliable/Jagged' at n=2 to 'Stable/Normal' at n=30.

sections.title: Real-World Application & Summary
sections.content: Summarize how CLT allows us to use Z-scores and confidence intervals to make inferences about massive populations using small, manageable samples. Final wrap-up on why CLT is the 'bridge' between probability and statistics.
sections.example: A Quality Control Robot in a factory measuring the average lifespan of lightbulbs to guarantee standards without destroying the entire batch.
